summary.text: The oxygen minimum zone is the ocean layer, roughly 200 to 1,500 m deep, where seawater's oxygen saturation is at its lowest.
Bacteria use up oxygen as they feed on organic matter raining down from above, and below the sunlit zone no photosynthesis replaces it.
Physical limits on mixing isolate this water into a pool where oxygen falls from the normal 4–6 mg/L to below 2 mg/L.

facts.label: Oxygen level
facts.value: Below 2 mg/L, versus a normal 4–6 mg/L

facts.label: Oxygen-free stretch
facts.value: Can stay anoxic for over 700 m of depth

items.prompt: Why does the very deep ocean, below the oxygen minimum zone, hold more oxygen than the layer above it?

options.label: Deep-sea plants release oxygen in the dark
Great pressure squeezes oxygen out of seafloor rock
Little is used there, and cold polar water brings more
Hot vents on the seafloor give off oxygen gas

items.explain: Oxygen consumption at great depth is low compared with the supply of cold, oxygen-rich water from polar regions.

items.prompt: A parcel of water at 800 m has had its oxygen used up by microbes. What must happen before that oxygen can be replaced?

options.label: The water must reach the surface ocean
The water must warm up by several degrees
Sunlight must filter down to that depth
The water must take on more salt

items.explain: Once oxygen in a parcel of water is consumed, it cannot be replaced without the water reaching the surface ocean.

items.prompt: Ocean water at the depth of the zone gets warmer. What happens to the amount of oxygen it can dissolve?

options.label: It goes up
It goes down
It stays exactly the same
It depends only on saltiness

items.explain: Colder water holds more oxygen, and rising ocean temperature reduces oxygen solubility.

items.prompt: When oxygen in the zone drops below 10 nM, microbes begin pulling elemental nitrogen out of nitrogen compounds. What happens to the ocean's nitrogen?

options.label: It builds up as extra nitrate
It is turned into fresh oxygen
It is locked away as seafloor rock
Some escapes as gas, so the ocean loses it

items.explain: Denitrification and anammox free elemental nitrogen, and what does not stay dissolved escapes as gas, a net loss for the ocean.

items.prompt: Two fish of the same species swim side by side in the same water: a small one and a large one. Which needs more oxygen for each gram of its body?

options.label: The large fish
The small fish
Both need exactly the same
Neither needs oxygen there

items.explain: Smaller organisms have higher metabolisms per unit of mass, so they need more oxygen per gram, while larger ones need more in total.

items.prompt: Wind blowing along a coast lifts nutrient-rich deep water to the surface. How does that help lower the oxygen further down?

options.label: The cold rising water pushes oxygen downward and out
The wind strips oxygen from the surface water
It fuels blooms whose sinking remains feed oxygen-using microbes
The nutrients react directly with dissolved oxygen

items.explain: Upwelled nutrients feed blooms; their sinking remains fuel microbes below the sunlit zone that use up the oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: The ocean's low-oxygen layer
paragraphs.text: The oxygen minimum zone, or OMZ, is the layer of the ocean where seawater carries the least oxygen; it is sometimes called the shadow zone. It lies somewhere between about 200 and 1,500 m down, depending on local conditions. OMZs occur around the world, typically off the western coasts of continents. There, oxygen falls from a normal 4–6 mg/L to under 2 mg/L, forming a kind of pool.

paragraphs.heading: Why the middle depths
paragraphs.text: Most of the falling organic matter, 80–90%, is eaten within the top 1,000 m. The deep ocean below stays richer in oxygen, because little is consumed there and cold, oxygen-rich water arrives from the polar regions. The middle depths get the worst of both: heavy consumption and a weak supply of fresh oxygenated water. In much of the ocean, mixing tops this layer back up, but in an OMZ physical barriers hold that mixing back.

paragraphs.heading: How a zone forms
paragraphs.text: Here is one example of how it can begin. Wind blowing parallel to a coast sets off Ekman transport and lifts nutrients up from deep water. The nutrients feed blooms of phytoplankton, grazing zooplankton and a busy food web at the surface. Their leftovers, from dead bodies and droppings to shed shells and scales, sink. Below the sunlit layer no photosynthesis makes oxygen, so microbes breaking down this debris draw the oxygen down. Depth then cuts the water off from mixing with the surface, while seafloor shape and large current systems block mixing from the sides.

paragraphs.heading: Where nitrogen escapes
paragraphs.text: In the heart of an OMZ, oxygen can fall below 10 nM, and the water can stay anoxic through more than 700 m of depth. At such low levels, microbial processes that oxygen normally blocks can run, such as denitrification and anammox. Both pull elemental nitrogen out of nitrogen compounds, and the part that does not stay dissolved escapes as gas. The ocean loses nitrogen as a result.

paragraphs.heading: What it means for animals
paragraphs.text: How much oxygen an animal needs depends on its metabolic rate, which shifts with water temperature and with the species, life stage, size and activity of the creature. Fish and invertebrates are ectotherms, meaning their body temperature follows the water's. When the water warms, their metabolism speeds up and they need more oxygen. Smaller animals need more oxygen for each unit of body mass, while bigger ones need more in total, and busier animals need more as well.
